content: In industrialized countries, sterilization procedures are most commonly performed using laparoscopy. However, in settings where resources for purchasing and maintaining laparoscopic equipment are limited, minilaparotomy remains a frequently used approach. The advantages and disadvantages of laparoscopic sterilization compared to minilaparotomy have not been systematically evaluated. The ideal sterilization method would be one that is highly effective, cost-efficient, can be performed on an outpatient basis, allows for a rapid return to normal activities, and results in minimal or no visible scarring. This review focuses on methods of accessing the abdominal cavity through the abdominal wall, regardless of the specific technique used for tubal sterilization. The objective of this review was to compare laparoscopic tubal sterilization with minilaparotomy in terms of operative morbidity and mortality. Additionally, trials comparing laparoscopy or minilaparotomy with culdoscopy were included. The review also considers different methods of interrupting tubal patency and the use of various forms of anesthesia, which will be addressed in separate reviews. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified using the Cochrane Collaboration's search strategy, and reference lists of identified trials were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria encompassed all RCTs comparing laparoscopy, minilaparotomy, and/or culdoscopy for tubal sterilization. The methodological quality of the trials and their appropriateness for inclusion were assessed. Data were independently extracted by reviewers, and results were reported as odds ratios for dichotomous outcomes and weighted mean differences for continuous outcomes. Six trials were included in the review. When comparing minilaparotomy to laparoscopy, there was no significant difference in major morbidity between the two groups. However, minor morbidity was significantly lower in the laparoscopy group (Peto OR 1.89; 95% CI 1.38, 2.59). The duration of the operation was also shorter with laparoscopy (WMD 5.34 minutes; 95% CI 4.52, 6.16). When comparing minilaparotomy to culdoscopy, major morbidity was higher in the culdoscopy group compared to the minilaparotomy group (Peto OR 0.14; 95% CI 0.02, 0.98). However, the duration of the operation was shorter with culdoscopy (WMD 4.91 minutes; 95% CI 3.82, 6.01). In the single trial comparing laparoscopy to culdoscopy, there was no significant difference in major morbidity between the two groups. However, significantly more women experienced minor morbidities with culdoscopy (Peto OR 0.20; 95% CI 0.05, 0.77). The authors concluded that major morbidity is a rare outcome for both laparoscopy and minilaparotomy. The choice of technique can be guided by the personal preference of the woman and/or the surgeon. Practical considerations, such as resource availability, must be taken into account before implementing endoscopic techniques in resource-limited settings. Culdoscopy is not recommended due to its higher complication rate.
